title: The Triple Test
question: Is 123,456 divisible by 3?
correctExplanation: Yes — digit sum 1+2+3+4+5+6 = 21, divisible by 3. Endings never decide threes.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is yes, digit sum 21. Threes care about digit sums, never final digits: 21 splits by 3, so 123,456 does. Endings govern twos, never threes.
lessonContent:
Threes read digit sums, never endings.
Add digits; test the total instead.
Endings govern twos, never threes.
Sums decide divisibility here.

title: The Square Eleven
question: Is 121 divisible by 11?
correctExplanation: Yes — 121 is 11 squared. Squares of eleven hide in plain sight.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is yes, 11 times 11. Primality claims fail: 11×11 = 121 exactly. Small squares deserve memorized spots.
lessonContent:
Small squares deserve memorized spots.
121 factors as eleven squared.
Primality claims need testing first.
Squares hide in round numbers.

title: The Famous Thousand
question: 1001 factors into which primes?
correctExplanation: 7, 11, 13 — 7×11×13 = 1001 exactly. The most useful thousand in puzzles.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 7, 11, 13. Test small primes: 7 divides (143), 11 divides that (13). Memorized factorizations pay compound interest.
lessonContent:
Memorized factorizations pay interest.
Test small primes systematically.
1001 splits three ways famously.
Famous numbers earn their fame.

title: The Nine Test
question: A combination lock opens only on multiples of 9. Dialed: 123456789. Does it click open?
correctExplanation: Yes — digit sum 45, divisible by 9. Size never blocks nines; sums decide.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is yes, digit sum 45. Add 1 through 9: 45 splits by 9, so the giant does. Largeness intimidates; sums adjudicate.
lessonContent:
Largeness intimidates; sums adjudicate.
Add 1-through-9 for 45 quickly.
Nines read totals, never sizes.

title: The Nines Check
question: A product's digit-sum check (casting out nines) disagrees with the written answer. What follows?
correctExplanation: The multiplication is wrong — casting nines never falsely accuses (mismatches prove error, matches merely suggest). Failed checks convict.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is the multiplication is wrong. Checks err on the side of caution only when passing: a failed casting convicts absolutely. Recompute, don't recheck.
lessonContent:
Failed castings convict absolutely.
Passing suggests; failing proves wrong.
Checks err toward caution only.
Recompute convicted products fully.

title: The Quarter Test
question: Is 1,234,568 divisible by 4?
correctExplanation: Yes — final two digits 68 split by 4 (17). Hundreds never matter for fours.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is yes, final two digits. 100 divides by 4 evenly, so only the last pair decides: 68/4 = 17 exactly. Endings decide fours completely.
lessonContent:
Hundreds never matter for fours.
Last pairs decide divisibility fully.
68 splits by 4 exactly here.
Endings rule quarters completely.

title: The Eighth Test
question: A warehouse ships crates only in multiples of 8. An order of 123,456 units arrives. Does it ship whole?
correctExplanation: Yes — final three digits 456 split by 8 (57). Thousands never matter for eights.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is yes, final three digits. 1000 divides by 8 evenly, so 456 alone decides: 456/8 = 57 exactly. Trios decide eights.
lessonContent:
Thousands never matter for eights.
Final trios decide divisibility.
456 splits by 8 exactly here.

title: The Zero Ending
question: Which of these is divisible by both 2 and 5?
correctExplanation: 4,444,440 — ending in zero satisfies both: even for 2, zero-or-five for 5. Zero endings pass double gates.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 4,444,440. Check endings: odd numbers fail 2 immediately; non-0/5 endings fail 5. Only zero-endings clear both gates at once.
lessonContent:
Zero endings clear double gates.
Endings decide twos and fives instantly.
Odd fails two; nonzero-five fails five.
Read last digits before dividing.

title: The Six Test
question: Which of these is divisible by 6?
correctExplanation: 222,222 — even (passes 2) with digit sum 12 (passes 3). Sixes need both gates cleared.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 222,222. Test 2 then 3: odd numbers (123,455; 45,679; 111,113) fail immediately; 111,113's sum 8 fails 3. Both gates, one survivor.
lessonContent:
Sixes need both gates cleared.
Even first, digit-sum second always.
Odd fails two instantly every time.
Double-gate tests need double checks.

title: The Dozen Test
question: An egg farm packs dozens exclusively, hating partial cartons. Which flock count packs perfectly?
correctExplanation: 144,444 — digit sum 18 (passes 3) with final pair 44 (passes 4). Dozens demand three-and-four together.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 144,444. Test 3 (sums: 19, 4, 24, 18) then 4 (endings: 57, 02, 81, 44): only 144,444 clears both. Twelve is three times four, always.
lessonContent:
Twelve is three times four always.
Sums then endings, in that order.
Both gates or no dozen entry.
Double tests need double passes.

title: The Fifteen Test
question: A shuttle seats 15; dispatchers hate partial loads. Which passenger count fills shuttles exactly?
correctExplanation: 77,775 — ends in 5 (passes 5) with digit sum 33 (passes 3). Fifteens need three-and-five together.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 77,775. Endings first: only 77,775 ends 0/5; sums second: 33 splits by 3. Fifteen is three times five, always.
lessonContent:
Fifteen is three times five always.
Endings first, sums second here.
Zero-or-five gates the test initially.
Thirty-three splits by three cleanly.

title: The Eighteen Test
question: A printer binds 18-page booklets; partial booklets jam the machine. Which page count runs clean?
correctExplanation: 325,674 — even (passes 2) with digit sum 27 (passes 9). Eighteens need two-and-nine together.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 325,674. Parity first (44,444 even but sum 20 fails 9; 123,456 even but sum 21 fails 9; 111,111 odd): only 325,674 clears both. Eighteen is two times nine.
lessonContent:
Eighteen is two times nine always.
Parity first, digit-sums second.
Twenty-seven splits by nine cleanly.

title: The Seventh Cycle
question: What six digits repeat forever in the decimal expansion of 1/7?
correctExplanation: 142857 — the cyclic number: multiples rotate its digits famously. Sevenths hide six-digit loops.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 142857. Long-divide 1/7: remainders cycle through six states before repeating. Memorized cycles beat repeated division.
lessonContent:
Remainders cycle before repeating fully.
Six states loop for sevenths.
Cyclic numbers rotate famously.
Memorize cycles, skip division.

title: The Thirteenth Cycle
question: Long-dividing 1/13, the remainder cycle produces a six-digit loop. Which loop emerges?
correctExplanation: 076923 — thirteenths cycle six digits: 13 × 76923 = 999999 exactly. Leading zeros count in cycles.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 076923. Sevenths lend 142857, but thirteenths run their own loop: divide 1/13 and watch 076923 recur. Leading zeros belong to cycles fully.
lessonContent:
Leading zeros belong to cycles.
Thirteenths loop six digits exactly.

title: The Long Cycle
question: How many digits long is the repeating block of 1/17?
correctExplanation: 16 digits — 17 is a full-reptend prime: periods stretch to denominator-minus-one. Long cycles hide in small primes.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 16. Seventeenths run the maximum period (p−1): sixteen digits before repeating. Full reptends reward patient division.
lessonContent:
Maximum periods reach p-minus-one.
Small primes hide long cycles.
Patience divides what memory skips.
Sixteen digits loop for seventeenths.

title: The Seven Rule
question: Is 203 divisible by 7? (Rule: double the last digit, subtract from the rest.)
correctExplanation: Yes — 20 − (2×3) = 14, divisible by 7, so 203 is too (29×7). Rules replace division cleanly.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is yes, 20 minus 6 is 14. Double-last-and-subtract tests sevens: 14 splits, so 203 (29×7) does. Endings never decide sevens.
lessonContent:
Double-last-and-subtract tests sevens.
Fourteen splits, so hundreds follow.
Rules replace division cleanly here.
Endings never decide sevenths.

title: The Repeated Block
question: Why does 237 × 1001 equal 237237?
correctExplanation: 1001 = 1000 + 1 — multiplying adds the number to its thousand-shifted self: abc000 + abc = abcabc. Structure, never coincidence.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 1001 equals 1000 plus one. Coincidence, rounding, and magic miss it: 237×1000 = 237000, plus 237 more. Addition explains repetition exactly.
lessonContent:
Structure explains repetition exactly.
Thousand-plus-one duplicates blocks.
Addition, never magic, repeats digits.
1001 splits usefully always.

title: The Six-Ones
question: 111,111 factors with a familiar 4-digit number. Which one?
correctExplanation: 1001 — 111,111 = 3 × 37 × 1001. Six ones hide the famous thousand.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 1001. Test small factors: 3 gives 37037, and 37 × 1001 completes it. Ones factor into familiar thousands.
lessonContent:
Ones factor into familiar thousands.

title: The Odd Palindrome
question: Four mirrored numbers face the eleven-test; three pass while one fails. Which palindrome breaks ranks?
correctExplanation: 12321 — alternating difference 1−2+3−2+1... precisely |2+3−4| = 1, not a multiple of 11. The others divide cleanly (1221, 1111, 2222).
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 12321. Alternating-sum test: 13431 (diff 0), 12221 (0), 24442 (0) all pass; 12321 gives remainder 1. One rebel among compliant palindromes.
lessonContent:
Alternating sums test elevens fast.
Zero difference means divisible here.
Rebels hide among compliant shapes.
Palindromes usually — not always — comply.

title: The Prime Test
question: Is 97 prime?
correctExplanation: Yes — test primes through √97 ≈ 9.8: 2, 3, 5, 7 all fail to divide. Primality confirmed by exhaustion.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is yes, it is prime. Check 7 (91, 98 bracket), 13 (too big alone... 13×7 = 91 ≠ 97), evenness, fives, threes: all fail. Exhaustion proves primality here.
lessonContent:
Exhaustion proves small primalities.
Test primes through square roots.

title: The Ninety-One Trap
question: Is 91 prime?
correctExplanation: No — 91 = 7 × 13, the classic prime impostor. Ends-in-1 numbers deserve factor checks.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is no, 7 times 13. Primality claims fail: 7×13 = 91 exactly. Impostors end in 1, 3, 7, 9 — check small factors always.
lessonContent:
Impostors end in 1, 3, 7, 9.
Check small factors unfailingly.
91 factors as seven-thirteen.

title: The Sum Clue
question: A number's digit sum is 27. Which divisibility is guaranteed?
correctExplanation: By 3 and 9 — 27 splits by both (9 and 3), and digit-sum rules inherit downward. Sums guarantee divisibility.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is by 3 and 9. Twenty-seven's factors transfer: whatever the sum allows, the number obeys. Sevens, elevens, and nones miss it.
lessonContent:
Sums transfer factors downward.
Twenty-seven splits both ways.
Guarantees ride digit totals.
Inherit divisibility from sums.

title: The Common Multiple
question: What is the smallest positive integer divisible by every number from 1 through 10?
correctExplanation: 2520 — 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 covers every prime power through 10. Least common multiple by max exponents.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 2520. Take highest prime powers ≤10 (8, 9, 5, 7) and multiply: 8×9×5×7 = 2520. Halves and doubles miss both ways.
lessonContent:
Max exponents build least multiples.
Prime powers through ten suffice.
2520 covers one through ten.
Multiply peaks, never all numbers.
